verdict_reasoning: The goal of NUMA-aware buffer placement has sustained developer interest, so level 1b does not fail for the series as a whole. Level 2 fails. maintenance-fit-1 and demand-1 show that the partitioning patches now depend on a replacement-policy change whose own author measured about 1% gain. maintenance-fit-2 shows a single-client loss with NUMA off. standards-compat-3 and replication-ondisk-1 show SIGBUS cases with no startup design.

brief.title: NUMA-aware shared buffers and partitioned clock-sweep
brief.problem: On multi-socket and multi-node machines, the kernel can place most of shared buffers on one NUMA node, for example after warmup by a single backend. This gives unpredictable performance and remote memory access, and the single clock-sweep hand is a contention point under buffer pressure. The target is large NUMA servers.
brief.proposed_design: The series splits shared buffers into a small registry of partitions and binds each partition, with its buffer descriptors, to a NUMA node on a best-effort basis at page granularity. Clock-sweep gets one hand per partition, a home partition per backend, balancing of allocations between partitions, and a scan of all partitions before failing. Greg Burd's later patches replace the 0..5 usage count with one second-chance bit, admit new pages on probation, and bound the work of one allocation.
user_visible_surface: GUCs shmem_populate and shmem_interleave (MAP_POPULATE, interleaving of the whole shared memory segment).
GUC shared_buffers_numa (default off) to bind buffer partitions to NUMA nodes.
pg_buffercache 1.8: new pg_buffercache_partitions view with clock-sweep and balancing counters.
Development GUCs: three clocksweep GUCs (including clocksweep_balance_recalc), debug_numa_node, and function pg_buffercache_set_weights(int, int[]).
pg_buffercache usagecount and pg_buffercache_usage_counts() now report only 0 or 1.
author_claims: Balanced placement makes results predictable and independent of how the cache was warmed.
Greg Burd measured +5-12% on seqconcurrscans with 2 nodes and +23-47% with 6 nodes; pgbench -S is flat on 2 nodes.
Single-client sequential scans regress, -12% on 2 nodes and -49% on 6 nodes, because each partition is too small for the table.
Partitioning alone makes the worst-case single allocation 4.1-4.6x worse on x86; the bound in 0006 removes this.
Best-effort page mapping wastes about one memory page per partition, which the authors call negligible.
brief.thread_state: Tomas Vondra, Jakub Wartak, Andres Freund and Greg Burd discussed it for over a year; Tomas reported regressions in June 2026, and Jakub's 0008 fixes and Greg's measurements followed. Open items include the c=1 regression, a partition size floor, crashes on CPU-less (CXL-like) nodes, and whether Greg's evictor changes belong in this series.
unclear: The material does not show whether Tomas agrees with merging the second-chance evictor into the series or with its reordering.
No design exists for CPU-less nodes, non-contiguous node IDs, or masks set by numactl or systemd.
The material does not say which GUCs are meant to ship and which are for development only.
No interaction plan with online resizing of shared buffers is given.
The material does not say how the huge page shortage on one node is detected; a FATAL exit was suggested but not shown.

prior_attempts.what_is_different: P4 reverted an unintended change to usage count increments on pin. This series replaces the usage count on purpose, so P4 only shows that such changes can disable buffer access strategies.

objections.title: Replacement-policy rewrite is bundled under the NUMA partitioning patches
objections.failure_scenario: A committer who wants only buffer placement and clock-sweep partitioning cannot take 0008-0012 without first taking 0004-0007. Those patches replace usage_count with one bit, add probation admission and add bgwriter behaviour. If a later release shows a workload whose hit ratio drops, the project has to revert the evictor and the partitioning together.
objections.argument: In message #108 the author of 0004 measured a gain of about 1% and wrote that the change is "not worth the potential risks". Message #109 then merged it, plus two new policy changes, ahead of the partitioning. Message #111 justifies the order by the 4x worst-case allocation that 0008 introduces alone, so the series now gives no NUMA step that can be committed without the evictor. Tools that read pg_buffercache usagecount also see their values collapse to 0 or 1.
objections.author_must_show: Can 0008-0012 stand on the existing 0..5 usage_count with their own fix for the worst-case allocation, so that the evictor change becomes a separate proposal?

critic.reasoning: Message #111 explains the order by the 4.1-4.6x worst case, but it does not say why the bound in 0006 needs the one-bit state. Message #108 judged the evictor not worth its risk, and the brief shows no agreement from Tomas.

objections.title: Partitioned clock-sweep costs users who never enable NUMA
objections.failure_scenario: A user on a single-socket box upgrades. That user gets four clock-sweep partitions by default and a per-allocation node lookup. A single-client report that scans a table larger than one partition, but smaller than shared_buffers, gets slower. The user finds out after the upgrade.
objections.argument: Message #98 reports 0004 with shared_buffers_numa=off at 114% of master latency at c=1. The 0002 commit message hard-codes 4 partitions independent of NUMA. Messages #106 and #107 show the c=1 loss rising to 49% as partitions shrink, and no partition size floor exists yet. Message #95 raises sched_getcpu() cost on every allocation, and only Jakub's 0012 caches it.
objections.author_must_show: With every NUMA option at its default on a non-NUMA machine, does the series behave like master for a single client scanning a relation between NBuffers/nparts and NBuffers/4?

critic.reasoning: Message #98 says the numa=off regression mostly recovers with later patches, and 0012 caches the node lookup. The c=1 loss from small partitions remains, because the minimum of 4 partitions applies without NUMA and no partition size floor exists.

objections.title: shared_buffers_numa does not follow NUMA limits set by numactl or systemd
objections.failure_scenario: An operator limits the instance to node 0 with numactl or systemd NUMAMask, or runs on a host with a CPU-less memory node. With shared_buffers_numa=on, the postmaster calls mbind() for every configured node. Startup then fails with SIGBUS, or shared buffers land on slow memory the operator had excluded.
objections.argument: Message #104 reproduces the SIGBUS on a CPU-less node and notes that the code counts nodes as 0..numa_num_configured_nodes() and ignores sched_getaffinity() and systemd masks. Message #105 agrees that the server should respect a NUMA limit the operator already set. Today numactl and systemd are the standard way to place a Postgres instance on NUMA hardware, so a setting that overrides them breaks deployments that work now. Message #97 suggested a FATAL exit when huge pages run short on a node, but the proposal does not show one.
objections.author_must_show: How does the series find the allowed node set, including non-contiguous, CPU-less, or masked nodes, and what does the server report when it cannot honour it?

critic.reasoning: Message #104 reproduces the SIGBUS on a CPU-less node and message #105 agrees that inherited masks should be respected. No later version in the material changes the node loop.

objections.title: Huge page shortage on one node can surface as SIGBUS after startup
objections.failure_scenario: An operator sizes nr_hugepages from shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages, and the kernel gives one node fewer pages than its partition needs. The server starts. Later a backend first touches a buffer bound to that node and gets SIGBUS, and the postmaster resets every session and runs crash recovery.
objections.argument: Message #94 reports that earlier versions crashed "much later" when one node ran out of huge pages. Message #75 leaves MAP_POPULATE commented out and still expects a small chance of SIGBUS. Message #104 shows the same failure on a CPU-less node. A FATAL exit at startup was suggested in message #97, but the material does not show it. A standby or failover target with a different per-node huge page layout would meet this at the worst moment.
objections.author_must_show: How does the server detect at startup that every bound partition can be backed on its node, and fail cleanly instead of with a later SIGBUS?

critic.reasoning: Message #75 reduces the risk by interleaving first but still expects a small chance of SIGBUS, and the FATAL exit from message #97 is not shown. The standby detail adds little, but the startup check is still missing.

objections.title: Replacing usage_count for all users lacks shown user benefit
objections.failure_scenario: Every installation, NUMA or not, gets a one-bit second-chance evictor with probation admission and bgwriter changes. Users and tools that read pg_buffercache usagecount find that it now reports only 0 or 1. A workload tuned under the 0..5 policy loses hit ratio after upgrade, and the user finds out only from a production regression.
objections.argument: In message #108, the evictor's own author measured about 1% more index leaf pages resident and TPS inside the noise. He concluded it was "not worth the potential risks" and said he would drop it unless someone else supported it. No one in the visible thread did, yet message #109 merges a broader version (0004-0007) ahead of the partitioning work. The main stated reason in message #111 is to fix a worst-case allocation regression that partitioning itself introduces, so this does not show demand for the evictor change on its own merits.
objections.author_must_show: Which workloads, outside fixing partitioning's own tail latency, gain measurably from the one-bit evictor, and who other than its author has asked for it?

critic.reasoning: Message #108 reports about 1% more leaf pages resident and TPS within run spread, and no other participant asked for the change. The benefit shown in message #111 is the removal of a regression that partitioning itself adds.

other_surviving.title: usagecount in pg_buffercache keeps its name but changes meaning
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool groups pg_buffercache.usagecount into 0..5 bands, or alerts on usagecount >= 3 as "hot". After upgrade the column only returns 0 or 1. The hot band reads empty, pg_buffercache_usage_counts() collapses to two rows, and nothing raises an error, so the operator sees a cache that looks cold.
other_surviving.argument: Message #109 calls usagecount and pg_buffercache_usage_counts() documented API, keeps their names and types, and changes them to report 0 or 1. Old queries still run but return different data, which is worse for users than a clear incompatibility. The change comes from the one-bit evictor, which message #108 judged not worth its risk for the performance gained, and which message #109 then merged into this NUMA series. Users would carry a visible break for an evictor change that has not yet shown a clear gain.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Why keep usagecount with a new 0/1 meaning instead of removing or renaming it, and does the second-chance evictor need to ship with this series at all?

critic.reasoning: Message #109 confirms the column and function keep their names and types but report only 0 or 1. The thread gives no reason for keeping the name beyond calling it documented API, so existing queries change meaning without an error.

other_surviving.title: No stated split between shipped GUCs and development-only knobs
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA reads about shmem_interleave, the clocksweep GUCs, or pg_buffercache_set_weights() and tunes production with them. A later release removes or redefines them, and postgresql.conf fails at startup with an unrecognized parameter, or the set weights stop working silently.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 says the GUCs were for development and not a final interface. Message #98 still folds the "goodies" patch into the series: three clocksweep GUCs, debug_numa_node, and a function that changes allocation weights across the server. Only debug_numa_node uses the debug_ prefix. The proposal does not say which settings are user-facing, what their defaults commit the project to, or who may call pg_buffercache_set_weights().
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which of these GUCs and functions are meant to ship as supported user settings, and why does each need to be user-visible?

critic.reasoning: Message #98 calls the extra GUCs useful for development, but the series still carries them and only debug_numa_node has the debug_ prefix. No message says which settings are proposed for commit.

refuted.title: Replacement-policy rewrite bundled as a prerequisite of NUMA partitioning
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes the partitioning work, and with it 0004-0007, which replace the 0..5 usage count with one bit, admit pages on probation and change bgwriter behaviour. A later workload loses hit ratio under the new policy. Reverting the evictor now also pulls out 0008-0012, which were rebased onto the one-bit state.
refuted.argument: [P6] was returned partly because it changed more than its goal needed. In message #108 Greg Burd measured the one-bit evictor at about 1% and said it was "not worth the potential risks". In message #109 the series nevertheless placed 0004-0007 ahead of Tomas's patches and made them a dependency. Message #111 defends this order because 0006 removes a 4.1-4.6x worst-case regression that 0008 introduces, but that bound could be added on top of the existing counter. The material shows no agreement from Tomas on the merge.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the allocation bound in 0006 sit on top of the existing 0..5 counter, so partitioning commits without changing the replacement policy, and if not, why not?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1, which makes the same bundling point without a precedent. [P6] concerns LWLock acquisition and must not be used as support here.

refuted.title: usagecount semantics and buffer state macros change without notice
refuted.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool or extension reads pg_buffercache.usagecount, or uses BUF_STATE_GET_USAGECOUNT from buf_internals.h, and treats values of 3 to 5 as hot buffers. After upgrade the extension fails to compile, or the dashboard shows the whole cache as cold, and nobody gets an error.
refuted.argument: Message #109 removes BUF_STATE_GET_USAGECOUNT, BM_MAX_USAGE_COUNT and the usage count bits, and keeps the documented usagecount column and pg_buffercache_usage_counts() with the same names but values 0 or 1. Same name with new meaning breaks consumers silently. Message #108 measured about 1% residency gain from the evictor change, so it is a weak reason for this break.
refuted.author_must_show: Why keep the usagecount name with new 0/1 meaning instead of a renamed column, and which extensions outside contrib read the removed macros?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1 for the usagecount column. The removed macros live in buf_internals.h, an internal header that carries no stability promise across major versions.

refuted.title: Privileges for pg_buffercache_set_weights and clocksweep runtime GUCs not stated
refuted.failure_scenario: A role granted pg_monitor or EXECUTE on pg_buffercache functions for monitoring calls pg_buffercache_set_weights with all weight on one partition, after clocksweep_balance_recalc has been turned off. Every backend then allocates from that one partition, and cache use and throughput drop cluster-wide. Operators find out from a regression they cannot trace to a session.
refuted.argument: The 0007 patch (message #98), later 0011, adds a function and three clocksweep GUCs that change shared allocation state for all backends at runtime. The material does not say whether the function is superuser-only, as pg_buffercache_evict is, or follows the read-only grants of the other pg_buffercache objects. It also does not give the GUC contexts for the clocksweep GUCs or for debug_numa_node. Message #98 calls these development aids, but they ship in the series, and the brief lists which ones ship as an open question.
refuted.author_must_show: Which roles can call pg_buffercache_set_weights and set the clocksweep and debug_numa_node GUCs, and are they superuser-only or removed before commit?

critic.reasoning: The scenario assumes grants and GUC contexts that the material does not show, and it needs clocksweep_balance_recalc turned off first. Message #98 presents these as development aids, so the open question is the one in standards-compat-2.

refuted.title: Startup depends on kernel NUMA and huge page layout with no design
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator runs on a host with a CPU-less CXL node, or with huge pages reserved on only one node. The postmaster calls mbind() on that node, and the server dies with SIGBUS during shared memory init or much later. The operator sees a crash with no Postgres-level message.
refuted.argument: Message #104 reproduces the SIGBUS on a CPU-less node. The same message notes that the code loops over 0..numa_num_configured_nodes() even though node IDs need not be contiguous or static. It also notes that cpusets and NUMAMask set by numactl or systemd are not respected. Message #96 calls the placement best effort, and the FATAL check proposed in message #97 is not shown. Each kernel or libnuma change in this area lands on whoever owns bufmgr startup.
refuted.author_must_show: What does the server do at startup with CPU-less nodes, sparse node IDs, an inherited node mask, or too few huge pages on one node, and how does each case fail?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-3 for the node set and of replication-ondisk-1 for the huge page shortage. The remark about future kernel or libnuma changes names no concrete case.

refuted.title: No plan for which of the new GUCs and functions ship
refuted.failure_scenario: A release ships shmem_populate, shmem_interleave, shared_buffers_numa, three clocksweep GUCs, debug_numa_node and pg_buffercache_set_weights(). Users then tune the balancing by hand. Any later redesign of the balancing has to keep these knobs working or break those configurations.
refuted.argument: Message #1 said the per-patch GUCs were for development only. Message #98 then added Jakub's "goodies" patch to the series. Message #94 says the balancing algorithm itself is still open, so its knobs would freeze an unsettled design. Ten such tuning surfaces per release would not be acceptable.
refuted.author_must_show: Which of these settings and functions are proposed for commit, and which stay out of tree?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-2, which asks the same question about which settings ship and has the more concrete failure scenario.

refuted.title: Balanced buffer placement repeats what numactl --interleave=all already gives
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator who wants warmup-independent placement already starts the postmaster under numactl --interleave=all or a systemd NUMAPolicy=interleave setting. With shared_buffers_numa=on they get the same even spread. Core still carries mbind code, the CPU-less-node SIGBUS cases from message #104 and per-node huge page checks, and the placement step adds no measured gain over interleaving.
refuted.argument: The stated goal in message #7 is predictable results independent of warmup, which OS interleaving already gives. The author's case for explicit placement over interleaving in message #1 was keeping a buffer and its descriptor on one node. Message #81 found no measurable effect from that, and message #101 says master must be benchmarked under numactl --interleave=all to compare fairly. Most of the measured gains come from the partitioned clock-sweep (messages #81, #106), which does not need explicit page binding.
refuted.author_must_show: With master started under numactl --interleave=all as the baseline, what does node-bound placement add beyond what the partitioned clock-sweep gives alone?

critic.reasoning: Interleaving cannot tell the sweep which node a buffer is on. Messages #90 and #93 show the locality gain needs node-bound partitions so a backend allocates local memory first, and message #102 reports results against an interleaved master.

refuted.title: shmem_interleave and debug_numa_node duplicate numactl options as GUCs
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator sets shmem_interleave=on while systemd or numactl already sets a memory policy. The two policies now overlap, and nothing in the proposal says which one wins. Each such GUC becomes a permanent setting that must track libnuma behaviour.
refuted.argument: Message #94 describes 0001 as "somewhat unrelated" and useful for benchmarking and as a baseline. Its commit message says it does what numactl --interleave does for the segment. debug_numa_node pins a backend to a node, which numactl --cpunodebind and systemd CPUAffinity already do. Message #104 asks to respect masks set by numactl or systemd, which fits poorly with also exposing GUCs that do the same thing. The brief notes that the material does not say which GUCs are meant to ship.
refuted.author_must_show: Which of shmem_interleave, shmem_populate and debug_numa_node are meant to ship, and what does each give that numactl or systemd settings cannot?

critic.reasoning: Message #10 explains that numactl --interleave also interleaves backend private memory, which shmem_interleave avoids by acting on the shared segment only. debug_numa_node carries the debug_ prefix, and the rest duplicates standards-compat-2.

refuted.title: Partitioned clock-sweep cost falls on everyone, gain on wide NUMA only
refuted.failure_scenario: A user on a 2-node or single-socket server upgrades and runs a large single-session scan or report. Each partition holds only a fraction of shared_buffers, so the table no longer stays resident. Message #106 measured this at -12% on 2 nodes and -49% on 6 nodes, and the user finds it as a slower nightly job.
refuted.argument: The 0003 commit message says clock-sweep partitioning applies even on non-NUMA systems, with a minimum of 4 partitions. The measured gains are on the synthetic seqconcurrscans workload only: +5-12% on 2 nodes and +23-47% on 6 nodes, while pgbench -S stays flat (message #106). The material has no field report or -general thread from users who hit clock-sweep contention. The partition size floor that would protect non-NUMA users is proposed in messages #106 and #107 but not designed.
refuted.author_must_show: What real workloads, from users outside the patch authors, are limited by clock-sweep contention, and what does a server with fewer than two sockets gain or lose by default?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2 for the cost on non-NUMA users. The demand part is weak, because several developers who know the buffer manager have worked on this problem for over a year.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: see objection replication-ondisk-1: Huge page shortage on one node can surface as SIGBUS after startup

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The series changes buf_internals.h and bufmgr.h, and pg_buffercache usagecount now reports only 0 or 1.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The series adds shmem_populate, shmem_interleave, shared_buffers_numa, three clocksweep GUCs and debug_numa_node.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: see objection maintenance-fit-2: Partitioned clock-sweep costs users who never enable NUMA

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: pg_buffercache_set_weights() changes allocation weights for all backends, and the proposal does not say who may call it.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The series adds partitioned clock-sweep, balancing, mbind-based placement and a new eviction policy in the buffer manager.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: Buffer allocation in freelist.c and bufmgr.c changes for every installation, with a minimum of 4 partitions without NUMA.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-3: shared_buffers_numa does not follow NUMA limits set by numactl or systemd

questions: Can the partitioning patches stand on the existing 0..5 usage count with their own bound on one allocation, so that the second-chance evictor becomes a separate proposal?
With every NUMA option at its default on a non-NUMA machine, does a single client scanning a relation larger than one partition perform like master?
How does the series find the allowed node set with CPU-less nodes, non-contiguous node IDs, or a mask set by numactl or systemd?
How does the server detect at startup that each bound partition has enough huge pages on its node, and fail with a FATAL message instead of a later SIGBUS?
Which of the new GUCs and pg_buffercache_set_weights() are proposed for commit as supported settings, and which are for development only?

committability.owner_note: Tomas Vondra wrote the base series and takes part in the thread. The owner must know the buffer manager and Linux NUMA and huge page behaviour.
committability.liability: The owner signs for buffer replacement behaviour on every installation, for startup failures tied to kernel NUMA and huge page layout, and for each shipped GUC, with no end date.
committability.author_follow_up: The authors have kept the series going for over a year, with rebases, regression reports and follow-up fixes through October 2026.

priority.reason: The target is large multi-node servers, and the series changes buffer allocation for everyone and adds kernel-dependent startup code. A committer is engaged, but the evictor bundling, the single-client regression and the node set handling need answers before code review.

provisional_note: Only 3 of 111 messages and the commit messages were read, so claims about later messages rest on the panel's reading. The cost of the allocation path with NUMA off and the SIGBUS handling cannot be judged without the code.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: [BUG] Assert fails for local buffers in BufferIsExclusiveLocked
precedents_retrieved.summary: The thread first asked whether BufferIsExclusiveLocked and BufferIsDirty need to handle local buffers, since only XLogRegisterBuffer calls them. After Andres Freund said local buffers must still be supported, the author proposed fixing the assertion in BufferIsDirty, which fails for local buffers because LockBuffer takes no content lock on them.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Andres Freund objected to dropping local-buffer support, but the author then changed the proposal to an assertion fix, and Nazir Bilal Yavuz said the patch looked good. Nazir also pointed to a similar thread started by Daniil, and the entry was withdrawn on the day it was registered.

precedents_retrieved.title: Default partition in list partitioning
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Robert Haas, Rushabh Lathia, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a DEFAULT partition to list-partitioned tables (FOR VALUES IN (DEFAULT)) so that rows matching no other partition are routed there instead of being rejected. The initial patch was preliminary, with pg_dump support, documentation, adding partitions after a default exists, and partition-key updates still to do.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was submitted late in the v10 cycle and was incomplete; reviewers found it did not compile cleanly, crashed the server when a partition was added after the default partition, and lacked test coverage and explanation of what was supported. The CF manager set a deadline for a new patch and marked the entry Returned with Feedback when it was not met; the updated patch arrived the same day and was immediately reported to fail on the original example. Robert Haas had already judged that it could not get into v10 because it was submitted at the last minute and not complete.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Considering that this patch was submitted at the last minute and isn't
even complete, I can't see this getting into v10.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix LWLock degradation on NUMA
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes LWLock acquisition so that a backend either takes the lock or takes the wait-list lock and sets LW_FLAG_HAS_WAITERS in one CAS loop, which removes the queue, recheck and dequeue sequence. It also makes contended LWLocks spin briefly before queuing, and it reworks LWLockWaitForVar in the same way.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry stayed in Ready for Committer for about a year and no committer took it up. Andres Freund said the patch changes more than the goal needs, and that removing the retry logic would block acquiring shared locks with a single lock xadd, which he found more efficient. Dmitry Dolgov returned it with feedback, citing lack of response and that comment; he also saw slight slowdowns in a virtual machine.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It changes a lot of things, more than I think are strictly
   necessary to achieve the goal.

precedents_retrieved.title: Extend more usecase for planning time partition pruning and init partition pruning.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch derives extra pruning quals for one side of a join from restriction clauses on the other side, using join equalities found in root->eq_classes or the joinlist for outer joins. This extends planning-time and init-time partition pruning to queries like p.partkey = q.colx with q.colx = $1 or q.colx = $2.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. All four messages are from the author, and no reviewer replied. The author posted a rebase on 2021-02-19, and the entry was withdrawn the same day without a stated reason.

precedents_retrieved.title: Extend more usecase for planning time partition pruning and init partition pruning.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch derives implied pruning quals for a partitioned table from join equalities such as p.partkey = q.colx combined with restrictions on q.colx (IN lists, OR clauses, range operators). These quals enable planning-time and init-time partition pruning, and partprune.c builds them on the fly and drops them after pruning.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said the implied quals should come from a general mechanism, so that EquivalenceClasses know about IN and btree range conditions and other planner parts such as index paths can use them. Code specific to partition pruning seemed wrong to them. That general approach needs faster lookup of expressions in EquivalenceClasses and care about planner overhead and redundant qual evaluation. The author said he was not prepared to do that work now and returned the entry himself.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It seems wrong to code anything in this regard that's specific to
partition pruning.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improved crc32c performance with AVX-512 algorithm.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an AVX-512 implementation of CRC-32C, ported from Intel ISA-L and Chromium code, for inputs of at least 256 bytes. Shorter inputs keep the existing SSE 4.2 code, with a run-time CPU check choosing the implementation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: John Naylor objected that AVX-512 needs complex hardware detection, helps only large inputs, and is missing from some current Intel server chips. He asked for a 128-bit carryless-multiplication version with a 64-byte minimum and a portable 3-way CRC technique, and raised an open question about Intel patents. Nathan Bossart had asked for the 14% regression on inputs under 256 bytes to be fixed. The author then moved to improving the SSE 4.2 code in a separate thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Complex hardware support (6 CPUIDs!) that only works on large inputs (a minority of workloads) looks to be the worst of both worlds and it's not the tradeoff we should make.

precedents_retrieved.title: Switch to FullTransactionId for PGPROC->xid and XLogRecord->xl_xid
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Matthias van de Meent, Michael Paquier, Robert Haas
precedents_retrieved.summary: As a step towards 64-bit XIDs, the patches change PGPROC->xid and XLogRecord->xl_xid from TransactionId to FullTransactionId. The author presented these as changes that any 64-bit XID design would need.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Making xl_xid 64-bit adds 4 to 8 bytes to nearly every WAL record, including records that need no XID, so all writes pay a WAL overhead. Reviewers said generic structures such as XLogRecord and PGPROC should not grow, and that a patch that makes things worse now should not go in for a later gain. Robert Haas also questioned the goal of 64-bit XIDs everywhere and asked to target the specific wraparound problems instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
And FWIW, echoing with Matthias, making these generic structures
arbitrary larger is a non-starter.  We should try to make them
shorter.

precedents_retrieved.title: Shared-memory based stats collector
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the file-based stats collector with statistics kept in dynamic shared memory (dshash), so backends read stats without a stats file written by a separate process. The stats collector process goes away, and per-kind stats code moves into new files under utils/activity.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reworked the patch in spring 2021 and judged it not committable for v14, citing weak test coverage, the need for architectural review and performance testing, an unresolved case where stats for dropped functions can be revived, and many open FIXMEs. A rebase then stalled on a new issue with partitioned tables. No new version was posted after July 2021, so the CommitFest manager marked the entry Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Unfortunately I think
that, while it has gotten a lot closer, it's still about a week's worth of
work away from being committable.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent shows NUMA buffer partitioning rejected before. Jakub Wartak's earlier NUMA entry, referenced in message #1, was returned in message #10 in favour of this approach, so it does not count against it.
Three objections are listed. The SQL syntax and pg_dump angles do not apply: the series adds no SQL-level objects and no syntax.
The series adds no WAL records, on-disk format or catalog state. Standbys and pg_upgrade are not affected beyond the two points above.

The core design, which places buffers on NUMA nodes and partitions clock-sweep, does not expose data or cross a privilege boundary. The new pg_buffercache_partitions view shows only allocation counters.
Not applicable. A committer (Tomas) and Andres are engaged, so ownership is less of a concern than design scope.
The partitioned clock-sweep itself has no existing equivalent in core or in an extension that I can name, so I raise nothing against it from this angle.

The NUMA placement part has independent developer interest: Jakub withdrew a competing patch, Andres has an earlier prototype, and two engineers ran measurements on 6-node hardware. These objections target only the parts whose cost lands on users who are not on NUMA hardware.
